claims.text: A controlled gradient microstructure containing stable high-entropy nano-precipitates will improve the mechanical strength of a refractory high-entropy alloy.
The same gradient nano-precipitate architecture will improve ductility.
The gradient nano-precipitate architecture will preserve high-temperature and irradiation stability.
The proposed baseline can be a W-based refractory high-entropy alloy with a relatively homogeneous microstructure.
The baseline alloy has only modest mechanical performance.
The W-based baseline has proven stability under high-temperature and irradiation conditions.
Thermo-mechanical treatment and nanoscale alloying can produce the proposed through-thickness gradient of stable nano-precipitates.
A gradient precipitate distribution promotes efficient load distribution.
The nano-precipitates impede dislocation motion and thereby increase mechanical strength.
Dilute, stable high-entropy precipitates preserve phase homogeneity through a high-entropy effect.
The high-entropy effect slows defect diffusion.
Increasing compositional complexity and entropy may improve helium-irradiation tolerance in refractory high-entropy alloys.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the modified alloy will have higher yield strength.
Relative to a homogeneous baseline, the modified alloy will have improved ductility.
The modified alloy will show no observable loss of phase stability.
The modified alloy will not show increased irradiation-induced defect accumulation relative to the homogeneous baseline.
The proposed benefits are expected to hold between approximately 800 and 1200 degrees Celsius and at reactor-relevant irradiation doses.
Nanoindentation can determine yield strength for the proposed comparison.

contradictions.description: The structural mediator requires a spatially varying distribution of embedded precipitates, whereas the mechanism says those precipitates preserve phase homogeneity. The intended meaning may be matrix-phase stability, but as written precipitate-induced heterogeneity and phase homogeneity are in tension.
